title: Why C is still worth learning
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what C gives you that higher-level languages hide, and why that layer keeps appearing in security work decades after people declared it obsolete.

blocks.text: In most languages, memory is somebody else's problem. You make a list, it grows; you stop using an object, it disappears. C removes that layer. You get the memory you asked for, exactly that much, and it stays yours until you give it back. Everything that follows in this course comes from that one difference.

C is a small language that maps closely onto what the machine does. There is no runtime deciding things on your behalf while the program runs, no automatic memory reclamation, and very little happening that you did not write. That makes it demanding, and it makes it predictable — which is why it is still where operating systems, databases, and embedded devices are written.

rows: You request it and you release it
It reads or writes whatever is there
Exactly the bytes you declared, in order
A garbage collector or virtual machine

blocks.title: The trade is real in both directions
blocks.text: This is not a claim that C is better. Memory-safe languages exist because manual memory management produces a well-documented class of bugs. The reason to learn C is that it makes the machine's actual behaviour visible — and that behaviour is still there underneath every language you use.
Where you will meet it whether you choose to or not

items: Operating system kernels, including the one on the machine you are reading this on
Databases, web servers, language runtimes — the fast parts of the stack your code sits on
Embedded and industrial devices, where there is no room for a runtime
Security work: exploitation, reverse engineering, and vulnerability research all happen at this level

blocks.title: Why this matters for security specifically
blocks.text: Memory-safety defects — reading past the end of a buffer, using memory after it was freed, arithmetic that silently wraps — have accounted for a large share of serious vulnerabilities in widely used software for decades, and industry and government analyses keep reporting the same pattern. You cannot understand those reports, or the mitigations built to stop them, without knowing what the code was doing to memory.
What C does not protect you from

blocks.caption: Three lines that compile without complaint
lines: numbers[10] = 42;        // past the end of the array — no error, no exception
p[0] = 'x';              // writing to memory you gave back
big = big + 1;           // undefined behaviour — in practice often a negative number, but nothing is promised

blocks.text: None of these stop your program at the moment of the mistake. Each one may work fine in testing and fail in production, or corrupt something quietly. Learning C means learning to see these before they happen — which is exactly the skill that transfers to reading someone else's code for defects.

blocks.title: Check that you can compile
steps: Run: gcc --version      (or: clang --version — either is fine)
If neither exists: on Debian/Ubuntu run sudo apt install build-essential; on macOS run xcode-select --install
Run: gcc check.c -o check && ./check && echo 'toolchain works'
Run: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O0 -g check.c -o check    (the flags this course will use)
blocks.expected: A compiler version, then a program that builds and runs with exit code 0. Those four flags will appear in every example: warnings on, no optimisation, debug information included.

cheatsheet: C gives you the memory you asked for and expects you to manage it
No runtime, no automatic reclamation, almost nothing happening you did not write
Out-of-range access is not an error in C — it reads or writes whatever is there
Kernels, databases, servers, and embedded devices are written at this level
Memory-safety defects are behind a large share of serious vulnerabilities
Signed integer overflow, use-after-free, and out-of-bounds access all compile silently

checkpoint.prompt: What is the fundamental difference between C and a memory-managed language?

choices.B: In C you request memory and release it yourself; there is no runtime reclaiming it for you
choices.D: C cannot allocate memory at runtime

checkpoint.explanation: That single difference is where the power, the danger, and most of this course come from.

checkpoint.prompt: What happens when C code writes past the end of an array?

choices.C: It writes into whatever memory is there — often with no visible symptom at that moment

checkpoint.explanation: There is no bounds check. The damage may appear much later, somewhere unrelated, which is what makes these bugs hard to trace.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is C central to security work even for people who write in other languages?

choices.A: Security tools are all written in C
choices.B: Memory-safety defects have accounted for a large share of serious vulnerabilities, and understanding them requires knowing what the code does to memory
choices.C: C is required for certification exams

checkpoint.explanation: Advisories, exploit write-ups, and the mitigations built to block them all describe behaviour at this level.

checkpoint.prompt: Why compile with -Wall -Wextra during this course?

choices.B: They turn on warnings, so the compiler tells you about suspicious code instead of silently accepting it
choices.C: They are required for the program to run

checkpoint.explanation: C accepts a great deal of questionable code by default. Warnings are the cheapest defect-finding tool you have, and most real C projects treat them as errors.
